title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
description: 1900 children's novel by L. Frank Baum
wiki_lead:
The Wonderful Wizard of Oz is a 1900 children's fantasy novel written by the American author L. Frank Baum and illustrated by W. W. Denslow. It is the first novel in the Oz series of books. A Kansas farm girl named Dorothy ends up in the magical Land of Oz after she and her pet dog Toto are swept away from their home by a cyclone. Upon her arrival in the magical world of Oz, she learns she cannot return home until she has destroyed the Wicked Witch of the West.
The book was first published in the United States in September 1900 by the George M. Hill Company. It had sold three million copies by the time it entered the public domain in 1956. It was often reprinted under the title The Wizard of Oz, which is the title of the successful 1902 Broadway musical adaptation as well as the iconic 1939 live-action film.
The ground-breaking success of both the original 1900 novel and the 1902 musical prompted Baum to write thirteen additional Oz books, which serve as official sequels to the first story. Over a century later, the book is one of the best-known stories in American literature, and the Library of Congress has declared the work to be "America's greatest and best-loved homegrown fairytale".

Publication

L. Frank Baum's story was published by George M. Hill Company. The first edition had a printing of 10,000 copies and was sold in advance of the publication date of September 1, 1900. On May 17, 1900, the first copy came off the press; Baum assembled it by hand and presented it to his sister, Mary Louise Baum Brewster. The public saw it for the first time at a book fair at the Palmer House in Chicago, July 5–20. Its copyright was registered on August 1; full distribution followed in September. By October 1900, the first edition had already sold out, and the second edition of 15,000 copies was nearly depleted.
In a letter to his brother, Baum wrote that the book's publisher, George M. Hill, predicted a sale of about 250,000 copies. In spite of this favorable conjecture, Hill did not initially predict that the book would be phenomenally successful. He agreed to publish the book only when the manager of the Chicago Grand Opera House, Fred R. Hamlin, committed to making it into a musical stage play to publicize the novel.
The play The Wizard of Oz debuted on June 16, 1902. It was revised to suit adult preferences and was crafted as a "musical extravaganza", with the costumes modeled after Denslow's drawings. When Hill's publishing company became bankrupt in 1901, the Indianapolis-based Bobbs-Merrill Company resumed publishing the novel. By 1938, more than one million copies of the book had been printed. By 1956, sales had grown to three million copies.

grok_lead: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz is a children's fantasy novel written by American author L. Frank Baum and illustrated by W. W. Denslow, first published on May 17, 1900, by the George M. Hill Company in Chicago. The story centers on Dorothy Gale, an orphaned farm girl living in Kansas with her Aunt Em and Uncle Henry, who is carried by a cyclone in her house to the magical Land of Oz, where it crushes the Wicked Witch of the East; there, with her dog Toto and new companionsâthe Scarecrow seeking brains, the Tin Woodman desiring a heart, and the Cowardly Lion craving courageâshe travels the yellow brick road to the Emerald City to petition the Wizard of Oz for help returning home. Baum crafted the tale as an original American fairy story intended solely to delight contemporary children, aspiring to modernize the genre by preserving wonder and joy while eliminating the explicit morals, cruel punishments, and nightmarish elements common in European folklore. Upon release, the book achieved rapid commercial success, with its initial run of 10,000 copies selling out within months and prompting reprints, ultimately inspiring Baum to produce thirteen Oz sequels during his lifetime. Its enduring legacy manifests in widespread adaptations across media, most prominently the 1939 Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer musical film The Wizard of Oz directed by Victor Fleming, which amplified global familiarity with Oz through innovations like Technicolor and songs such as "Over the Rainbow," though it altered book details including the silver shoes becoming ruby slippers. Although Baum eschewed didactic or political purposes, the narrative has attracted interpretive controversies, notably a 1964 essay by Henry Littlefield positing it as an allegory for 1890s Populismâequating the yellow brick road to the gold standard, silver shoes to bimetallism advocacy, and characters to economic archetypesâbut this view has been challenged by scholars and Baum biographers for lacking evidence in the author's correspondence, political activities, or explicit statements, suggesting instead an overimposed academic reading rather than causal authorial intent.
